label: Morning edition
summary: Keanu, **the AI rout ended Friday with tech's worst week since 2020**: the S&P 500 and Dow closed in correction, the Nasdaq fell 5.28% and about 10% on the week, and Anthropic closed at $88.91, just above its $83 IPO price (CNBC, Axios, Fox Business). Nvidia fell about 14% after Reuters reported the SEC is exploring accounting issues, its seventh straight weekly loss (CNBC). In Washington, **four senators will oppose a stopgap without Iran war limits**, with the Dec. 11 funding deadline ahead (NPR, The Hill, Fox News). Iran struck two more ships and hit targets in Kuwait and Bahrain, and October set a record for attacks on shipping (NPR, NBC News). Schumer leads Van Hollen in public counts before the Dec. 1 leadership vote (The Hill, Axios, Washington Examiner). Locally, **drizzle this weekend gives way to an atmospheric river** Tuesday night through Thursday, with 1 to 3 inches of rain and record-threatening tides (SF Chronicle, KQED). California's analyst warned that an AI-driven crash could mean **a $35 billion annual deficit** (CalMatters, KQED). Webb data helped reconstruct a star spiraling into a giant companion in Andromeda (NASA, Nature).

stories.title: Democrats split over using the Dec. 11 funding deadline to force limits on the Iran war
stories.summary: Four senators say they will oppose a stopgap without war limits, while House Democrats avoid shutdown threats and Republicans warn of a holiday shutdown.
story: Congress returns after Thanksgiving with a Dec. 11 deadline, when the stopgap passed in September runs out, and the Iran war is the main obstacle (NPR, The Hill, Fox News). Democratic Sens. Michael Bennet, Tammy Duckworth, Bernie Sanders and Chris Van Hollen say they will vote no on a stopgap that lacks language restricting the administration from spending funds on the war. Sen. Tim Kaine is drafting a provision to that effect. Majority Leader John Thune called the demand 'short-sighted' and warned it could sink any deal (The Hill).

The math is hard for both sides. A stopgap needs 60 votes, and Republicans hold 53 Senate seats, so they need about seven Democrats (The Hill, Fox News). Axios reports House Democrats are mostly steering clear of December shutdown threats, and Rep. Jim McGovern said he would try to defund the war in January if he cannot in December. Schumer wants the war to end but is described as wary of overplaying his leverage.

On the Republican side, the Pentagon is pushing a $350 billion party-line package, and The Hill reports it is meeting GOP resistance. Fox News says the administration's cost estimates have ranged from $50 billion to $200 billion and that fiscal hawks want offsets. The Washington Examiner reports that Republicans are unwilling to force an end to the war despite their midterm losses. Sen. John Kennedy said that if Democrats tie funding to 'cutting and running,' there will be a shutdown (Fox News).
Democrats take control of both chambers in January, so the December deal is the last one written under Republican control (Fox News).
facts: The current stopgap funds the government through Dec. 11 (NPR, Fox News).
Bennet, Duckworth, Sanders and Van Hollen said they oppose a stopgap without Iran war limits (The Hill).
A Senate stopgap needs 60 votes; Republicans hold 53 seats (Fox News).
The Pentagon is pushing a $350 billion party-line defense package (The Hill).
No deal or shutdown has been reported yet (NPR, The Hill).
stories.left: The war was never authorized by Congress, and voters just handed Democrats both chambers partly because of it. The power of the purse is the one tool the Constitution gives Congress to end an open-ended conflict. A Reuters/Ipsos poll cited by Newsweek found 71% of Americans want legislation ending the war. Democrats argue that funding it again without limits would ignore the election result.
stories.right: Cutting off money while U.S. troops are under fire in Kuwait and Bahrain would endanger service members and reward Tehran's attacks on shipping. Republicans argue that a shutdown hits air traffic controllers, troops and holiday travelers first and does nothing to stop Iran. National security funding should not be a hostage, and Democrats who threaten a shutdown will own the consequences, as Thune and Kennedy have put it.
stories.next: The Senate Democratic leadership vote on Dec. 1 and the Dec. 11 funding deadline set the pace; watch whether Kaine's provision gets a vote.

stories.title: Republicans split on Trump's warmth toward Xi and Putin after the Shenzhen summit
stories.summary: The trilateral talks produced a declaration with no word on Ukraine or Iran, and reactions at home cut across party lines.
story: A week of fallout continues from President Trump's Thursday meeting in Shenzhen with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin. The leaders signed a joint declaration pledging dialogue on reducing nuclear risks, stable energy supplies and United Nations reform, and it made no mention of Ukraine or the Iran war (Fox News, The Hill). Trump rated the meeting 'a 12' on a scale of zero to 10 and called the relationships built 'fantastic' (Fox News).

Democrats were sharply critical. Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer called it a 'historic embarrassment' (NBC News), and Rep. Gregory Meeks, the top Democrat on House Foreign Affairs, told NPR he did not think much was done and feared talk of spheres of influence that sideline allies. Sen. Jeanne Shaheen wrote that Trump's 'friend' is 'a murderous war criminal' after Trump used the word for Putin (NBC News). Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk replied, 'God, protect us from such friends' (Fox News).

Republicans were not uniform. Sen. Bill Hagerty called the meeting a 'healthy thing,' while Sen. Jim Banks said China and Russia are not our friends (The Hill). Vice President JD Vance defended direct engagement, arguing diplomacy is critical to protecting American interests (Fox News). The Washington Examiner ran an op-ed arguing Beijing staged the event to flatter Putin while keeping the upper hand.
Fox News also reported that Chinese officials barred a Bloomberg reporter from the meeting after she asked about Nvidia's Jensen Huang.
facts: The meeting took place Thursday in Shenzhen, China, on the sidelines of the APEC gathering (Fox News).
The declaration covered nuclear risk dialogue, energy supplies and UN reform and did not mention Ukraine or Iran (Fox News, The Hill).
Trump said 'I think it was a 12' (Fox News).
Chinese officials barred a Bloomberg reporter from the meeting after a question about Jensen Huang (Fox News).
Hagerty and Banks, both Republicans, gave opposite verdicts (The Hill).
stories.left: The summit gave two adversaries a stage and America got almost nothing in return. Calling Putin a friend while Russia shells Ukraine undercuts allies, and Poland's prime minister said as much. A declaration that skips Ukraine and the Iran war suggests the three leaders are discussing a carve-up of influence, as Meeks warned, and Congress should demand answers about what was discussed.
stories.right: Talking to adversaries is not appeasement, and Vance made the case that diplomacy protects American interests. Republicans who defend the trip argue that nuclear risk reduction and energy stability are real topics worth a seat at the table. Skeptical conservatives such as Banks warn that warm words are cheap and that Xi and Putin must be judged by actions, a point the Washington Examiner's op-ed makes with some force.
stories.next: Watch whether any Ukraine talks follow and whether Congress asks what was discussed in Shenzhen.

stories.title: Schumer holds a public lead over Van Hollen as the Senate Democratic leadership vote nears
stories.summary: Public tallies favor Schumer, but the secret ballot and a large undecided group leave room for surprise.
story: Sen. Chris Van Hollen is challenging Chuck Schumer for Senate Democratic leader in a secret-ballot election scheduled for Dec. 1, right after the Thanksgiving recess (The Hill, Axios). Schumer says he has the votes. Public counts differ by outlet: Axios counted 14 senators publicly behind Schumer, himself included, and five behind Van Hollen, while The Hill's whip list showed 16 and six, with 34 undecided. The Washington Examiner counted 15 for Schumer and four for Van Hollen.

Van Hollen says he has 'more than 10' senators with him, though few have said so in public (The Hill). Bernie Sanders and Elissa Slotkin back him (Fox News). John Fetterman opposes him over his views on Israel (Fox News). Van Hollen is running on a populist platform that includes ending the filibuster and Medicare for All (The Hill). Hillary Clinton called the challenge a 'performance, in a way' and said she expects Schumer to survive (Fox News).

The winning threshold is 28 or 29 votes, depending on how Alaska's Senate race is resolved (The Hill). Allies of Schumer predict he will get more than 40 votes. Some Democrats, including Sen. Mark Kelly, discussed moving the vote earlier, while Van Hollen argued against rushing it (The Hill).
The contest overlaps with the Iran war funding fight, since Van Hollen is also among the senators demanding war limits in the stopgap.
facts: The vote is a secret ballot on Dec. 1 (The Hill, Axios).
Axios counted 14 public Schumer backers to five for Van Hollen; The Hill counted 16 to six with 34 undecided.
Sanders and Slotkin back Van Hollen (Fox News).
The threshold is 28 or 29 votes depending on the Alaska race (The Hill).
Challenges to the party's Senate leader had not happened in 32 years (Axios).
stories.left: Democrats just won both chambers on an anti-establishment mood, and Van Hollen's supporters argue the party needs a leader who will fight harder on the war, costs and the filibuster. They say a caucus that wants to channel voter anger should not hand the gavel to the same strategy that lost ground for years. Van Hollen's backers also note that a secret ballot lets senators vote their conscience.
stories.right: Conservative writers see a Democratic caucus pulled toward its left flank, with a challenger endorsing Medicare for All and ending the filibuster. The RNC called the fight a preview of 'chaos, infighting' under Democratic control. Republicans note that even Democrats such as Fetterman worry about Van Hollen's positions and see the race as proof that moderate voices are losing influence in the party.
stories.next: Senators vote Dec. 1; watch whether the date moves up and how many senators back Van Hollen in the secret ballot.

stories.title: Light rain this weekend, then an atmospheric river and record-threatening tides before Thanksgiving
stories.summary: Fremont sees drizzle Saturday and Sunday, while the National Weather Service expects 1 to 3 inches Tuesday night through Thursday.
story: The Bay Area gets a break from heavy rain this weekend, then faces a bigger storm in Thanksgiving week (SF Chronicle, KQED). The SF Chronicle forecasts a cold, wet weekend with highs in the mid- to upper 50s, showers possible Sunday morning and totals under a quarter inch. Saturday daytime and Sunday afternoon look like the best windows to be outside. Data from live.json show a Fremont high of 55 on Saturday and 54 on Sunday, with a low chance of rain Saturday.

The main concern is an atmospheric river arriving Tuesday on top of the year's highest tides. The SF Chronicle reports the National Weather Service expects 1 to 3 inches of rain between Tuesday night and Thursday, though the timing and location are uncertain. Tides could reach the 3 to 3.5 foot range if the storm lines up, which would beat the previous record of 2.98 feet, and breaking waves of up to 25 feet are possible on Pacific beaches (SF Chronicle).

Marin officials are urging residents to avoid nonessential travel during high tide next week, and some communities may face evacuation warnings (SF Chronicle). KQED has a guide to how the storm could affect Thanksgiving travel, which includes Tuesday and Wednesday, the peak travel days. The Fremont forecast shows a 64% chance of rain on both days.
facts: Fremont highs are 55 Saturday and 54 Sunday (live.json).
Weekend rain totals are expected to stay under a quarter inch (SF Chronicle).
The National Weather Service expects 1 to 3 inches Tuesday night through Thursday (SF Chronicle).
Tides could top the 2.98-foot record (SF Chronicle).
Fremont has a 64% rain chance Tuesday and Wednesday (live.json).
stories.flag: Exact rain totals and tide heights for next week are still uncertain and will shift with updated National Weather Service forecasts.
stories.next: Check updated forecasts Monday; the peak Thanksgiving travel days are Tuesday and Wednesday, Nov. 24 and 25.

stories.title: California analyst warns an AI-driven market crash could mean $35 billion annual deficits
stories.summary: The Legislative Analyst sees a small gap in a mild slowdown and a gap the state cannot cover if stocks fall sharply.
story: California's nonpartisan Legislative Analyst's Office (LAO) released its fiscal outlook this week and warned that the state's budget is tied to an AI-fueled stock market (CalMatters, KQED, SF Chronicle). In a gradual slowdown the state faces a $2 billion deficit by the end of fiscal 2027-28, growing to $15 billion a year by 2028-29. In an abrupt downturn in 2027, the annual gap could reach $35 billion by 2028-29, and the state would not have enough reserves to cover it (CalMatters).

The report marks the fifth straight year of projected deficits despite revenue growth, and CalMatters says the state now carries nearly $30 billion in debt. Governor-elect Xavier Becerra takes office Jan. 4 and must submit his first budget soon after. Cuts to health care for undocumented immigrants take effect next year unless he finds new money. He has signaled openness to new taxes without giving specifics, and his spokesperson says he will deliver a 'responsible, balanced budget' (CalMatters).

The warning landed in a week when the Nasdaq lost 10% and erased its 2026 gain, which gives the crash scenario new weight (CNBC). KQED describes the crash risk as potentially pushing annual deficits past $30 billion.
facts: The LAO outlook came out this week (CalMatters, KQED).
The base case is a $2 billion gap by 2027-28 and $15 billion a year by 2028-29 (CalMatters).
The crash scenario is a $35 billion annual gap by 2028-29 (CalMatters).
Becerra takes office Jan. 4 (CalMatters).
California has projected a deficit five years in a row (CalMatters).
stories.left: California has been prudent about reserves, and Democrats note the state's revenue depends on high earners and capital gains that rise and fall with markets. Many progressives argue this volatility is an argument for broadening the tax base, including taxes on very high wealth, rather than cutting health care and safety net programs. They point out that the deficit is partly a revenue problem.
stories.right: Conservative critics say a fifth straight deficit shows Sacramento has built spending on temporary money and market windfalls. They argue the state should cut growth in spending now, rather than raise taxes that drive high earners and employers out of California. A budget that only balances while Nvidia and Anthropic stock climbs, they say, is not a plan, a point Becerra will have to answer.
stories.next: Becerra's first budget proposal is due in January; watch the Dec. 7 start of the new Legislature for early moves.
stories.blindspot: No right-leaning outlet coverage of the LAO report turned up; sources are center and left-leaning outlets.

stories.title: Iranian attacks on ships hit wartime highs as Tehran targets U.S. sites in Kuwait and Bahrain
stories.summary: Iran struck two ships in one day while the U.S. blockade holds, and October set a record for attacks on shipping.
story: Iran struck two ships in a 24-hour period this week, an oil tanker and a gas carrier, and the gas carrier exploded, NPR reported. October saw more attacks on ships in the Strait of Hormuz than any month since the war began in late February, and November is on pace to exceed it (NPR). The U.S. is escorting ships through the strait along Oman's coast and maintains a naval blockade of Iranian ports, and attacks continue anyway (NPR, Fox News).

Iran also widened its attacks on U.S. sites. Iran's military said it targeted Ali Al Salem Air Base in Kuwait and sites in Bahrain, after a U.S. strike on an Iranian missile site on Qeshm Island. Kuwait's military said its air defenses intercepted drones and did not immediately report damage (NBC News, The Hill). Outlets differ on the day, with AP and The Hill saying Wednesday and Fox News saying Tuesday.

Iran's Revolutionary Guard claimed it hit navigation and radar equipment on Oman's Didamar Island, which Omani officials dispute (Fox News). A CNN analyst called the situation an 'unstable status quo,' and some experts read the attacks as a sign Tehran is tired of the blockade (CNN, NBC News). No casualty figures from the latest Kuwait strike turned up in the reports.
facts: Iran struck an oil tanker and a gas carrier within 24 hours, and the gas carrier exploded (NPR).
October had more ship attacks than any month since the war began (NPR).
Iran said it targeted Ali Al Salem Air Base in Kuwait (NBC News, The Hill).
Kuwait said it intercepted drones and reported no immediate damage (The Hill).
WTI crude is $83.41, up 1.18% (live.json).
stories.left: The war has no congressional authorization and has now run for nearly nine months with ship attacks at record levels, which shows military escorts and a blockade have not delivered security. Critics say the escalation is the predictable result of a policy without an exit and that renewed diplomacy, including enforcing the existing memorandum, is the way out.
stories.right: Iran's attacks on commercial ships and U.S. bases show why the blockade and escorts are needed. Conservative analysts argue that the pressure is working, as the economy suffers and Tehran lashes out in frustration, and that backing away now would reward aggression and let Iran control a global oil chokepoint.
stories.next: Watch for casualty reports from Kuwait and Bahrain, and whether Congress ties war funding to the Dec. 11 deadline.

stories.title: Tech has its worst week since 2020 as the S&P 500 and Dow end in correction and Anthropic gives back its IPO pop
stories.summary: The Nasdaq fell 5.28% Friday and about 10% on the week, with Nvidia down 23% and Anthropic at $88.91.
story: U.S. stocks ended a punishing week with another rout Friday. The S&P 500 fell 3.70% to 6,910.39, the Dow fell 1.93% to 48,147.33 and the Nasdaq fell 5.28% to 22,617.73, which erased the Nasdaq's 2026 gain and left the S&P and Dow in correction territory (CNBC, Fox Business, NPR). The Nasdaq slid about 10% over five sessions, its worst week since early 2020 (CNBC, Axios).

Nvidia dropped about 14% Friday and 23% on the week, its sharpest weekly pullback in 18 years and a seventh straight weekly loss (CNBC). Anthropic closed its second day of trading at $88.91, down 8.5%, only slightly above its $83 IPO price and well below its $111.50 opening trade Thursday (CNBC, Axios). CNBC lists five forces behind the selloff: the Anthropic IPO, Nvidia's troubles, fears the Fed is losing the inflation fight, data center backlash and export-control scrutiny. The 10-year Treasury yield fell to 4.91% as investors looked for safety (live.json).

For next week, CNBC says traders expect more volatility. The S&P's relative strength index fell below 30, a technical sign of oversold conditions that can precede a bounce, and strategist Katie Stockton advises against selling into weakness. The Stock Trader's Almanac says the low is more likely in mid- to late December. U.S. markets are closed Thursday for Thanksgiving (CNBC).
facts: The S&P 500 closed at 6,910.39, down 3.70% (live.json).
The Dow closed at 48,147.33, down 1.93% (live.json).
The Nasdaq closed at 22,617.73, down 5.28% (live.json).
Anthropic closed at $88.91 after opening at $111.50 on its first day (CNBC, Axios).
The 10-year Treasury yield was 4.91% and WTI crude $83.41 (live.json).
stories.why: A selloff led by the companies spending the most on AI hits retirement accounts and state budgets, including California's. Whether Nvidia's guidance of about 75% growth next year holds up under scrutiny will decide if this is a reset or a bust.
stories.next: Markets reopen Monday, Nov. 23, with a shortened Thanksgiving week and the Fed meeting on Dec. 8-9.

stories.title: Chase, Apple, the NSA and the FAA each blame their own software or maintenance for last week's outages
stories.summary: Officials see no cyberattack, while Nadella says much critical infrastructure is unpatchable.
story: A string of outages hit banks, air travel, the NSA and Apple earlier this week, and the companies and agencies each gave a different cause (CNBC, NPR, Axios). JPMorgan said longer service times at Chase came from a software bug in on-premises hardware systems. Apple said an internal update caused its disruption and denied a cyberattack, with its status page showing everything resolved by 6 PM ET Tuesday. The NSA said its issue happened during scheduled routine maintenance and did not affect mission-critical capabilities.

The FAA cited a router upgrade in southern Arkansas overseen by contractor L3Harris Technologies that overwhelmed its telecommunications network. A flood of traffic destabilized older legacy equipment (CNBC). Secretary of State Marco Rubio said there is 'zero' evidence the outages were connected or tied to rival nations or criminals (NPR).

Skeptics are not satisfied. Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella said at the New York Times DealBook Summit that much critical infrastructure, such as firmware, chillers and HVAC systems, is 'unpatchable' yet connected to the internet, and he called the Outlook outage the result of a 'latent bug' (TechCrunch). Nadella argued that as AI speeds up vulnerability discovery, patches must reach production almost instantly, which he expects to create instability. Axios reports the FBI said an AI hacking tool called Artex was used to breach networks in under three hours, and one defense CEO called the outages a 'taste' of future attacks, which is his view, not established evidence (Axios).
Lawmakers are calling for more transparency about each incident.
facts: Chase blamed a software bug in on-premises hardware systems (CNBC, Axios).
Apple blamed an internal update and denied a cyberattack (CNBC).
The NSA cited scheduled routine maintenance (CNBC).
The FAA cited a router upgrade by L3Harris in southern Arkansas (CNBC).
Rubio said there is 'zero' evidence of a connection (NPR).
stories.why: Four unrelated failures in a week show how fragile complex systems are when patching speeds up. If AI keeps compressing the time between a vulnerability and an exploit, fast patching and brittle legacy systems collide.
stories.next: Watch for formal after-action reports from the FAA and JPMorgan, and any congressional hearing on resilience.

stories.title: Webb data show a star spiraling into a giant companion in the Andromeda galaxy
stories.summary: The Nature paper uses the event, named Bao, to directly measure how efficiently a common envelope ejects gas.
story: Astronomers led by Viraj Karambelkar of Columbia University reported in Nature on Nov. 18 that an eruption in the Andromeda galaxy, AT 2025abao, came from a smaller star spiraling into a larger one (Nature, NASA, Space.com). The Zwicky Transient Facility caught the eruption on Oct. 17, 2025, and earlier hints showed up in NEOWISE data from 2023 and SPHEREx data from July 2025 (Nature).

NASA's James Webb Space Telescope observed the system 47 days after the eruption peaked, which NASA calls the earliest follow-up of this kind. Its mid-infrared data let the team trace the companion, about 0.7 solar masses, falling into a roughly 7 solar mass giant star and ejecting gas and dust. Estimates put the expelled material at about 0.1 to 0.2 solar masses.

The team says this is the first time telescope data has directly measured the efficiency of common envelope evolution, a stage that shapes how many close binary stars, including the progenitors of gravitational wave sources, form. Karambelkar has said a second reading remains possible, in which both stars survive in a much tighter orbit, so a full merger is the leading interpretation and not the only one.
facts: The paper is in Nature, volume 659, published Nov. 18, 2026 (Nature).
The Zwicky Transient Facility detected the eruption on Oct. 17, 2025 (Nature).
Webb observed 47 days after the peak (NASA).
The companion is about 0.7 solar masses and the primary about 7 (Nature).
Ejected material is about 0.1 to 0.2 solar masses (Nature).
stories.why: Common envelope phases are central to how close binaries become compact objects, but models relied on guesses for how efficiently gas leaves. One well-observed event turns that from theory into a measurement.
stories.next: Astronomers will keep watching the remnant with Webb to tell a full merger from a tighter surviving pair.

stories.title: Nvidia faces an SEC probe and a California subpoena as it posts record sales under its interim CEO
stories.summary: Scrutiny of the chipmaker widens after Jensen Huang's exit, even as its latest quarter beat estimates.
story: Nvidia shares fell about 14% Friday after Reuters reported the SEC is exploring potential accounting issues at the company, according to CNBC. The Wall Street Journal had reported Tuesday that the SEC was opening a civil probe into whether Nvidia's disclosures misled investors (CNBC, TechCrunch). Neither Nvidia nor the SEC has publicly confirmed an investigation in the results found. CNBC says the stock was on track for its seventh straight weekly loss, the longest such streak since 2008.

The pressure follows CEO Jensen Huang's resignation on Nov. 12 amid reports of an affair with a woman U.S. intelligence reportedly believes is a Chinese spy. Finance chief Colette Kress is interim CEO (CNBC, TechCrunch). California Attorney General Rob Bonta issued an investigative subpoena as part of a probe into whether advanced Nvidia chips reached China in violation of export rules (CNBC). Huang is due to appear before House committees in December (CNBC).

The business itself looks strong. Nvidia reported fiscal third-quarter revenue of $115.84 billion on Nov. 17, up 103% and above the $109.11 billion consensus, and Kress guided to about $130 billion for the fourth quarter and roughly 75% growth next year, up from 70% (CNBC, Fox Business). She said Vera Rubin is 'off to an explosive start.' TechCrunch's headline was that Nvidia 'promises that revenue will keep soaring, for now.'
facts: Nvidia fell about 14% Friday and 23% on the week (CNBC).
Reuters reported the SEC is exploring possible accounting issues; the WSJ reported a civil probe Tuesday (CNBC).
Huang resigned Nov. 12; Colette Kress is interim CEO (CNBC, TechCrunch).
California's attorney general subpoenaed Nvidia in a China chip diversion probe (CNBC).
Fiscal Q3 revenue was $115.84 billion, up 103% (CNBC).
stories.why: Nvidia is the clearest bellwether for AI spending, and a leadership and legal crisis at the same time as record sales makes it hard to separate business risk from governance risk. A probe into disclosures could take months.
stories.next: Watch Huang's House testimony in December and any formal SEC or Nvidia statement on the probe.
stories.flag: Neither the SEC nor Nvidia has confirmed an investigation in the reports found; the accounts rest on Reuters and WSJ sourcing.

stories.title: Newsom pushes a tiered AI kill switch and keeps a special session on the table
stories.summary: A report recommends a procedure to shut down dangerous models, and legislation could come when lawmakers return Dec. 7.
story: Gov. Gavin Newsom released a report in Washington, D.C., this week recommending a tiered 'kill switch' procedure that would give California the power to temporarily shut down AI models found to be dangerous, KQED and the SF Chronicle reported. Newsom said his team is already preparing legislation to carry out the framework. He vetoed a similar measure, SB 1047, in 2024 (KQED, CalMatters).

Newsom has not called a special session. He said 'all options are on the table' and that the answer is yes 'if the conditions come together,' but they 'have to come together quickly' (SF Chronicle). The new Legislature convenes Dec. 7, and Gov.-elect Xavier Becerra takes office Jan. 4. Newsom said he wants to be sensitive to Becerra, who has not committed to the guidelines (CalMatters).

Republican gubernatorial candidate Steve Hilton calls a kill switch a 'gimmick' (CalMatters). The SF Chronicle frames the push as Newsom positioning himself as a national AI safety leader ahead of a likely 2028 run. The proposal arrives in a week when AI stocks fell sharply, and the targets include Anthropic and OpenAI releases, KQED said.
facts: The report recommends a tiered kill-switch procedure for dangerous models (KQED, SF Chronicle).
Newsom has not called a special session (SF Chronicle).
The new Legislature convenes Dec. 7 (SF Chronicle).
Becerra takes office Jan. 4 (CalMatters).
Newsom vetoed SB 1047 in 2024 (CalMatters).
stories.left: Frontier labs say their systems are powerful enough to be dangerous, so a shutdown authority is a reasonable backstop, like a recall power for unsafe products. Supporters say California is the state where these companies are based and should write the rules the federal government has not.
stories.right: Critics, including Hilton, call a kill switch a gimmick that adds compliance cost without making anyone safer, and warn it could push AI firms out of California or hand a future governor leverage over private companies. Conservatives also ask who decides what counts as dangerous and under what evidence.
stories.next: Watch whether Newsom calls a special session before Dec. 7 and what bill language appears.

briefs: The U.S. officially lost its measles elimination status after the Pan American Health Organization found the virus circulated for more than a year, and CDC director Erica Schwartz said 'Vaccination does' protect Americans (NPR).
SpaceX is still investigating why Starship Flight 15's booster aborted its tower catch even though the ship was caught Nov. 14 (Space.com).
The BART board chose Pacific Development and Affirmed Housing to build 643 homes, 176 of them affordable, on parking lots at the Fremont station (SF Chronicle).
Euclid discovered its first comet, C/2026 S1, orbiting between Jupiter and Saturn (Space.com).
Science reports researchers controlled a virtual fruit fly using a map of the insect's brain (Science).
